title: A peaked curve is a mechanism question: why hydrogen and efficiency rise and then fall with steam
summary: Hydrogen yield, cold-gas efficiency and combustion-zone temperature are all plotted against the same steam-to-fuel ratio, with and without a catalyst. Read them as one story: they peak at the same ratio, which points to temperature as the thing that changes, and not steam alone.

media.alt: Line chart with error bars of hydrogen yield in volume percent dry against steam-to-biomass ratio SBR from 0 to 0.47 for lignite with steam (blue circles) and lignite with 7 percent MgCO3 and steam (orange squares). Both curves rise to a sharp peak near SBR 0.25, about 32.5 and 34.7 percent, then fall; the catalytic curve falls below the no-catalyst curve at high steam.

source.caption: H2 yield vs steam-to-biomass ratio (non-monotonic finding)
group: 01_02_h2_vs_sbr: H2 yield vs steam-to-biomass ratio (non-monotonic finding)
05_25_tcomb_vs_sbr_energy_balance: Combustion-zone temperature explains the H2 non-monotonicity
source.note: Group explainer for the three headline plots. The SBR axis is labelled kg steam per kg fuel; the fuel is lignite, although captions say biomass. The Pearson correlations quoted in the caption of figure 05 are reproduced below from values read off the figures.

read_the_figure.question: How do hydrogen yield, cold-gas efficiency and combustion-zone temperature change with the steam-to-fuel ratio, and does the catalyst change the shape or only the level?
read_the_figure.axes: x: steam-to-biomass ratio SBR in kg steam per kg fuel, 0 to about 0.47 (seven runs per series). y: figure 01, H2 in vol% dry, with error bars (about plus or minus 0.5); figure 02, cold-gas efficiency in percent, no error bars; figure 05, combustion-zone temperature in degrees C, solid for measured values and dotted for a first-law energy-balance prediction.
look_at: Blue is lignite plus steam, orange is lignite plus 7% MgCO3 plus steam, in every figure. Circles and squares mark individual runs.

The peak: both series peak at SBR about 0.25 in all three figures. In figure 01 the peak is a single run per curve, 32.5 (no catalyst) and 34.7 vol% (catalyst); its neighbours are about 3 to 9 points lower.

The levels: the catalyst raises cold-gas efficiency at every SBR (figure 02, by about 12 points on average) but raises H2 only up to the peak; at SBR 0.3 and above the catalytic curve is below the no-catalyst curve in figure 01.
Figure 05: the dotted prediction falls steadily with SBR (steam dilutes and cools), the solid measurement does not. The title says a coarse first-law balance does not reproduce the rise.
The x positions of the two series differ slightly (for example 0.43 against 0.47 at the right end), so points at the 'same' SBR are not exactly paired.
read_the_figure.proves: That the response of H2 yield and of efficiency to steam is non-monotonic over the range tested, that the maximum lies near SBR 0.25 for both conditions, and that the combustion-zone temperature has the same shape. It does not prove a mechanism: a correlation across seven runs per series is a hypothesis.
if_wrong: A peak that rests on one point: a single bad run would create or remove the effect. Replicates or error bars on the neighbours are needed.
Series that are not run at equal conditions other than SBR: the next explainer (operating map) shows that the equivalence ratio also changes between runs.
Efficiency without error bars while yield has them: the two cannot be compared at the same level of confidence.
must_check: What error bars mean (replicates, instrument error, or standard deviation of a time window).
The same runs underlie the three figures; the x positions match between figures 01, 02 and 05.
Definition of SBR and of the efficiency (what heating values are used).
That other controls (air flow, feed rate, temperature) were not changing together with steam.
Whether the dotted prediction is a model or a hand balance, and what it assumes about heat loss.
as_drawn: Rise from SBR 0 to the peak: 32.5 / 24.1 = 1.35 (no catalyst), 34.7 / 26.1 = 1.33 (catalyst). Fall from the catalytic peak to SBR 0.47: 23.2 / 34.7 = 0.67.
Cold-gas efficiency (figure 02, percent): no catalyst 66, 68, 70, 73, 75, 69, 62; catalyst 81, 82, 85, 85, 87, 78, 68.

Combustion-zone temperature measured (figure 05, degrees C): no catalyst 743, 766, 812, 831, 831, 785, 745; catalyst 787, 807, 830, 854, 909, 831, 768. The dotted energy-balance prediction falls from about 997 to 710 (no catalyst) and from 906 to 636 (catalyst).

Correlation of H2 with combustion-zone temperature from these read-off values: 0.73 for no catalyst, 0.96 for the catalyst, 0.80 pooled; H2 with SBR pooled: 0.10. These match the values quoted in the caption of figure 05 (0.80, 0.96, 0.10), computed here independently.

The caption of figure 05 says the temperature 'explains' the H2 non-monotonicity; the figure's own title says the coarse balance does not reproduce the temperature rise. The correlation says the two move together, not why the temperature rises.

terms.meaning: Mass of steam fed per mass of fuel. On the axis it is labelled steam per fuel; the fuel here is lignite.
Here the volume percent of H2 in the dry product gas, not the mass of H2 per kg of fuel.
The chemical energy in the product gas (at room temperature) as a fraction of the chemical energy in the fuel.
CO + H2O to CO2 + H2, mildly exothermic (about -41 kJ/mol). Favoured by steam and by lower temperature.
The measured temperature in the part of a downdraft gasifier where air burns part of the fuel and supplies the heat for the rest.
A curve that rises then falls; the optimum is inside the tested range.
A number between -1 and 1 for how closely two quantities follow a straight-line relation.
A 7 percent mass fraction of magnesium carbonate mixed with the lignite, tested as a catalyst; the figure labels it as such.

remember: A peak inside the tested range means the 'more steam is better' rule fails: there is an optimum.
Steam is a heat sink: more steam cools a gasifier unless something else compensates.
Correlation across seven points is a clue, not a mechanism.
Water-gas shift moves toward H2 with more steam and less heat.
r squared is the fraction of variance a straight line explains.

understand.title: Why the three plots belong together
understand.text: Hydrogen yield, efficiency and temperature all peak at about the same SBR. When three measures share a turning point, one underlying variable is likely driving them. Temperature fits: it controls both the rates and the shift equilibrium.

understand.title: Why steam is double-edged
understand.text: Steam brings hydrogen into the reaction (more water to react) but also absorbs heat to warm up and to drive endothermic steps. At low SBR the first effect wins; past the optimum the cooling does. The dotted line is the cooling effect alone.

understand.title: What the catalyst does
understand.text: The catalyst lifts the whole efficiency curve and the H2 curve up to the peak. After the peak the catalytic curve drops faster than the other; whatever the catalyst does, it does not widen the useful range of steam.

steps.title: Define the ratio
steps.note: A mass ratio. The seven runs per series span 0 to about 0.47.

steps.title: Cold-gas efficiency
steps.note: The product-gas flow times the heating value of its combustible species (H2, CO, CH4) over the fuel's heating value.

steps.title: A first-law estimate of the temperature
steps.note: With a fixed heat release and more steam in the total flow, the temperature must fall: this is the dotted prediction in figure 05. A measured rise needs another effect (for example the heat from shift or better combustion) that this balance does not contain.

steps.title: Water-gas shift
steps.note: More steam pushes the equilibrium toward H2; the reaction releases a little heat, so cooler gas favours it too.

steps.title: Pearson correlation
steps.note: A straight-line measure. A peaked response has r near zero against its own driver, which is why the pooled H2-against-SBR value is only 0.10 although the curves clearly respond to SBR.

steps.title: Variance explained
steps.note: The pooled temperature explains about 64 percent of the variance of H2, the catalytic series about 92 percent. With seven points per series these are descriptive, not tests.

worked.title: Rise and fall of the catalytic H2 curve
worked.problem: Read the catalytic H2 values 26.1 at SBR 0, 34.7 at SBR 0.26 and 23.2 at SBR 0.47 (vol%). What are the relative rise and fall, and at what SBR is the gain over the no-catalyst case largest?

solution.text: The gain over the no-catalyst curve at the peak is 34.7 - 32.5, while at SBR 0 it is 26.1 - 24.1.

worked.answer: A 33 percent rise and then a 33 percent fall; the catalytic gain is about 2 points at both ends of the rising branch and turns negative past SBR 0.3 (26.1 against 29.3). All values are read off the figure.

analyze.q: Each curve has one point at the peak. How would you test whether the peak is real?
analyze.hint: Repeat that run, add runs at SBR 0.22 and 0.28, and compare with the error bars.

analyze.q: Why does the pooled H2 against SBR correlation come out near zero although H2 clearly depends on SBR?
analyze.hint: Think of a curve that goes up and down.

analyze.q: The dotted prediction and the measured temperature agree at SBR near 0.2 and then diverge. What could the extra heat in the measurement be?
analyze.hint: Think of exothermic steps that the coarse balance omits.

evaluate.q: The caption says temperature 'explains' the H2 curve. Rewrite it so that it claims only what the figures support.
evaluate.hint: Correlation, same turning point, no tested causation.

evaluate.q: Does the catalyst help? Answer for H2 and for efficiency separately.
evaluate.hint: Compare the two curves at every SBR.

create: Design the next run set that would separate steam from temperature: hold the combustion-zone temperature fixed by adjusting air while sweeping steam.
Redraw figure 02 with error bars and with the same x positions as figure 01, so the three figures can be overlaid.

checks.q: Why does steam both help and hurt hydrogen yield?
checks.hint: Think of reactant and heat sink.
checks.answer: It supplies the water for the shift and steam-reforming reactions, but it must be heated and drives endothermic steps, which cools the reaction zone.

checks.q: H2 goes from 24.1 to 32.5 vol% between SBR 0 and the peak. What is the relative increase?
Three different quantities peak at the same SBR. What does that suggest?
checks.answer: That a single driver, probably the combustion-zone temperature, controls all three; it is a hypothesis to test.

checks.q: A pooled correlation of 0.10 between H2 and SBR. Does it mean SBR does not matter?
checks.answer: No: Pearson r measures straight-line association, and an up-then-down response has almost none, even though SBR clearly changes H2.

checks.q: What run would test the temperature hypothesis directly?
checks.hint: Break the link between steam and temperature.
checks.answer: Vary steam at constant measured combustion-zone temperature, by trimming the air supply, and see whether the H2 peak disappears.
